Pandas is a Python data handling package built on the NumPy package.

Installation: pip install pandas or conda install pandas

Fortunately we will not need this, since the Anaconda distribution already contains it. The version number of the current installation can be queried through Python.

import pandas as pd
print(pd.__version__)

1.3.3

On the Pandas website many useful descriptions are available, but it is also worth looking at the built-in documentation (help(pd)).

The other files used during the practical:

  • kosar.csv
  • kosar.json
  • imdb.csv
  • szeged.csv
  • olimpia.csv
  • covid.csv

Data structures

The two data structures of Pandas that we too use a great deal are the dataframe (data table) and the series (data series).

It is worth looking up the documentation of both (pd.DataFrame, pd.Series)

Data series

The pandas data series (Series) was devised for storing one-dimensional data, but the more complex data structures are also built out of them.

They are created starting from traditional Python lists.

import pandas as pd
a_list = ['apple', 'pear', 'lemon']
ds = pd.Series(a_list)

print(f"List:\n{ds}\n")
print(f"Indices(keys):\n{ds.index}\n")
print(f"Values:\n{ds.values}\n")

List:
0    apple
1     pear
2    lemon
dtype: object

Indices(keys):
RangeIndex(start=0, stop=3, step=1)

Values:
['apple' 'pear' 'lemon']

The Pandas index is like the address of a house (not only in the case of a Series). With its help we can select data points from the whole database or from a column. Both the rows and the columns have an index: the index of the rows is the index, while the index of the columns is the name of the column. A good index contains only distinct values. In most cases this is a sequence of numbers increasing by one; a time series index is also often used, but they can also be overwritten with arbitrary values.

import pandas as pd
a_list = ['apple', 'pear', 'lemon']
index_list = ['x', 'y', 'z']
ds = pd.Series(a_list, index=index_list)

print(f"List:\n{ds}\n")
print(f"Querying values:\n{ds[0]}\n{ds['y']}\n")

List:
x    apple
y     pear
z    lemon
dtype: object

Querying values:
apple
pear

Data table

The pandas data tables (DataFrame) store the data in named columns.

Because of the structure, creating data tables requires a data structure more complex than a simple list. The input of the data table is a Python dictionary in which the names will be the names of the columns and the values are the lists containing the values of the corresponding columns. An important stipulation is that the lengths of the lists cannot differ from one another.

import pandas as pd

data = {
    'apple': [3, 2, 0, 1], 
    'orange': [0, 3, 7, 2]
}
df = pd.DataFrame(data)

print(f"Data table:\n{df}\n")
print(f"Indices(keys):\n{df.index}\n")
print(f"Column names(fields):\n{df.columns}\n")
print(f"Values:\n{df.values}\n")
print(f"Querying a column:\n{df['apple']}\n")
print(f"Querying several columns:\n{df[['apple', 'orange']]}\n")
print(f"Querying values:\n{df['orange'][2]}\n")

Data table:
   apple  orange
0      3       0
1      2       3
2      0       7
3      1       2

Indices(keys):
RangeIndex(start=0, stop=4, step=1)

Column names(fields):
Index(['apple', 'orange'], dtype='object')

Values:
[[3 0]
 [2 3]
 [0 7]
 [1 2]]

Querying a column:
0    3
1    2
2    0
3    1
Name: apple, dtype: int64

Querying several columns:
   apple  orange
0      3       0
1      2       3
2      0       7
3      1       2

Querying values:
7

The example above shows how the individual values of the data table can be queried. From the structure it is perhaps also clear that data tables are essentially made up of named data series. To any (even empty) data table we can append a further column by giving the column name and the data series.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['apple'] = pd.Series([3, 2, 0, 1])
df['orange'] = pd.Series([0, 3, 7, 2])
df.index = ['Anna', 'Ben', 'Cecil', 'David']

print(df)
print('\n')
print(df['orange'])

       apple  orange
Anna       3       0
Ben        2       3
Cecil      0       7
David      1       2


Anna     0
Ben      3
Cecil    7
David    2
Name: orange, dtype: int64

The example also shows that the data table handles a common index which sets the index of every data series appearing in it. A data series already indexed differently from the standard can overwrite the original indexing. The new index containing plain numbers can be created with the reset_index() function. In this case – unless we specify otherwise in a parameter – the old index becomes a column.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['apple'] = pd.Series([3, 2, 0, 1])
df['orange'] = pd.Series([0, 3, 7, 2])
df.index = ['Anna', 'Ben', 'Cecil', 'David']

print(df)
df = df.reset_index()
print()
print(df)

       apple  orange
Anna       3       0
Ben        2       3
Cecil      0       7
David      1       2

   index  apple  orange
0   Anna      3       0
1    Ben      2       3
2  Cecil      0       7
3  David      1       2

It also often happens that we want to query a whole row of a data table (in database terminology: one of its records). We can do this using the loc property. Using iloc we can still use the original ordinal index even if it has been overwritten.

import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame()
df['apple'] = pd.Series([3, 2, 0, 1])
df['orange'] = pd.Series([0, 3, 7, 2])
print(df.loc[1])

print()
df.index = ['Anna', 'Ben', 'Cecil', 'David']
print(df.loc['Cecil'])
print()
print(df.iloc[1])
print()
print(df.loc['Ben':'David'])

apple     2
orange    3
Name: 1, dtype: int64

apple     0
orange    7
Name: Cecil, dtype: int64

apple     2
orange    3
Name: Ben, dtype: int64

       apple  orange
Ben        2       3
Cecil      0       7
David      1       2

As can be seen, when querying rows the multiple selection possibilities familiar from lists can also be used, but here the handling of the end of the intervals differs.

File operations

Creating a data table from a file

One of the greatest advantages of pandas is that with a few simple instructions it is able to process the contents of several kinds of source file suitable for handling tables. The result in every case is a data table.

The files needed for the following examples can be downloaded from the list above. The examples assume that the downloaded files are located next to the program file.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('kosar.csv')
print(df)

  Unnamed: 0  apple  orange
0       Anna      3       0
1        Ben      2       3
2      Cecil      0       7
3      David      1       2

Files often contain key fields. By giving the appropriate parameter, pandas is able to handle these.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('kosar.csv', index_col=0)
print(df)

       apple  orange
Anna       3       0
Ben        2       3
Cecil      0       7
David      1       2

Processing JSON files works similarly. But in this case, if there is an index column, it has to be determined on the basis of the name of the column.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_json('kosar.json')
df = df.set_index('index')
print(df)

       apple  orange
Anna       3       0
Ben        2       3
Cecil      0       7
David      1       2

Writing a data table to a file

The contents of the previous examples can just as easily be written out into files of the appropriate type. In this way even converting files can easily be solved.

If we write the results into a subdirectory, the folder has to exist, otherwise the writing will run into an error.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_json('kosar.json')
df = df.set_index('index')
df.to_csv('new_basket.csv')

Of course the other direction works too.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('kosar.csv', index_col=0)
df.to_json('new_basket.json')

Data table operations

In what follows we present the operations of the pandas module using the data of an IMDB database stored in CSV.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')
print(df)

Basic descriptive operations

The head function lets us easily take a look at the data structure. It returns the number of rows of the table passed as a parameter. (In the absence of an argument the default value is 5.)

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')
print(df.head())

This is useful when reviewing large data tables, because in this way Python does not try to display all the data rows unnecessarily.

The tail function works in the same way, but it returns the last rows.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')
df.tail()

The shape property contains the size of the dimensions of the table. The info function gives a summary of the data structure of the table. And describe describes the various statistical measures of the numeric variables. The corr function shows the correlation of the numeric values with one another.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')
print('SHAPE')
print(df.shape)
print('\nINFO')
print(df.info())
print('\nDESCRIBE')
print(df.describe())
print('\nCORRELATION')
print(df.corr(numeric_only=True))

Sorting a data table

The sort_values function sorts the rows of the data table on the basis of the values of the column(s) given in the by parameter. (For sorting by index the sort_index function is the one to use.) Another new thing in the code below is that the various functions can be chained onto one another, where, moving from left to right, the input variable of every function is the result of the previous function.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

df = df.sort_values(by=['Year', 'Rating'], ascending=False)
print(df.head(10))

Rows / records

Data tables generally store the data of a list of some kind of entities. The columns determine the properties stored, and the rows (otherwise known as records) describe the concrete properties of one entity each (e.g. student, product).

Adding rows

The rows of a data table can be extended in a number of ways, but here we review only a few simpler possibilities. To extend the table we simply have to refer to a non-existent index and assign a value to it.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df.tail())

new_line = {
    'Rank': 1001,
    'Genre': 'Romance'
}
df.loc['Titanic'] = new_line

last_line = df.iloc[-1]
df.loc[df.index[-1] + ' 2'] = last_line
print(df.tail())

When assigning a value, the properties can be described on the basis of the dictionary data structure above, and a new row can be created. It is important that in the present example we do not have numeric indices but have used the titles as identifiers, so the new record has to be referred to by the title of the new film when adding it. Fortunately it is not compulsory to fill in every piece of data, but it is advisable.

Of course we rarely create a new record manually; rather we request all the data on a form, or generate a new one precisely by modifying existing rows. In the example above we query the truncated element added last and create the record representing the second part of the film. It is worth noting that to produce the second title the last_line variable cannot be used, because the indices belong to the original table; the queried row no longer knows what its index was in the original table.

It often happens, however, that we have to insert not just one but several records into a table.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')
df2 = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

df2.index = df2.index + ' 2'

df3 = pd.concat([df, df2])
print(df3)

In the example above we loaded the data set a second time as well, but in the second round we overwrote the indices so that there would be no clash. Then we merged the two tables using the concat function. Any number of tables can be merged in this way, and the correspondence of the columns does not have to be complete, but it is very important that there be no repetition in the indices. In the help many special parameters can be found that assist with the handling of the indices.

Deleting rows

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df.head())
df = df.drop(['Split', df.iloc[4].name])

print(df.head())

For deletion the drop function can be used, and the elements can be identified by the index of the given records. In the example above we deleted the films 'Split' and 'Suicide Squad'.

If several elements have to be deleted at once, then instead of deletion it is worth filtering the data set on the basis of conditions (see later).

Columns / data series

The columns correspond to the properties of the individual entities. Every column is a data series, that is, essentially a list storing the values belonging to the corresponding indices.

Adding columns

Columns can be extended even more simply than rows, since there is no need to bother with the indices for them, but in exchange one has to pay attention to the number of elements.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df)
df['Counter'] = range(len(df))
print(df)

In the example we appended a counter column to the table by assigning a value while referring to a non-existent column name. In practice columns are rather produced with various operations (see later) using the already existing ones, so meeting the number of elements mostly does not cause a problem.

Deleting columns

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df.columns)
df = df.drop(columns=['Rank'])
print(df.columns)

Index(['Rank', 'Genre', 'Description', 'Director', 'Actors', 'Year',
       'Runtime (Minutes)', 'Rating', 'Votes', 'Revenue (Millions)',
       'Metascore'],
      dtype='object')
Index(['Genre', 'Description', 'Director', 'Actors', 'Year',
       'Runtime (Minutes)', 'Rating', 'Votes', 'Revenue (Millions)',
       'Metascore'],
      dtype='object')

Operations

With the dataframe['column_name'] syntax we can select a column. In this way we get a Pandas data series. By contrast, with the dataframe[['column_name']] syntax we narrow the data table down to one (or more) column, but its format remains a data table.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df['Rating'])
print(df[['Rating']])

The unique function lists the set of values of the given column. The max and min functions show the largest and the smallest value. And the idxmax and idxmin functions show the index belonging to these values. The sum, median, mean etc. functions return the corresponding value as one would expect. The quantile function shows the percentage quantile given in the q parameter. E.g. q=.2 -> 20%

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df['Rating'].unique())
print(df['Rating'].max())
print(df['Rating'].min())
print(df['Rating'].idxmax())
print(df['Rating'].idxmin())
print(df['Revenue (Millions)'].sum())
print(df['Year'].median())
print(df['Year'].mean())
print(df['Year'].quantile(q=.2))

The code below uses the fillna function to write the average revenue into the missing values.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

revenue = df['Revenue (Millions)']
revenue_mean = revenue.mean()
print(revenue_mean)
revenue.fillna(revenue_mean, inplace=True)
print(revenue)

print(df['Revenue (Millions)'] / df['Runtime (Minutes)'])

Selecting values with conditions

On the basis of certain conditions we can filter our data. In the background the condition checks for every piece of data whether the statement is true or false. Combined with the loc property we can then filter the data table.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')
condition = (df['Director'] == 'James Gunn')
print(condition.head())

print(df.loc[condition])

Title
Guardians of the Galaxy     True
Prometheus                 False
Split                      False
Sing                       False
Suicide Squad              False
Name: Director, dtype: bool

The condition can also be numeric and less/greater than, but we can join several conditions with the OR (|) and AND (&) operators, together with appropriate bracketing. With the df['column_name'].isin(a_list) function we can filter for those values that appear in a_list. Below a multiply compound system of conditions can be seen. The formatting helps to show which bracket belongs where.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')
result = df.loc[((df['Year'] >= 2010) & 
       (df['Year'] <= 2015)) & 
       (df['Rating'] > 8.0) & 
       (df['Revenue (Millions)'] < df['Revenue (Millions)'].quantile(0.25))]
print(result)

Listing empty values

The isnull function shows which value is missing. The sum function counts up the data gaps identified in the foregoing: False = 0 and True = 1. With the dropna function we drop those rows where there is an empty value.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df.isnull())
print(df.isnull().sum())
print(df.dropna().isnull().sum())

Group by

There is often a need for a data query that aggregates the individual values grouped along some property. The group by feature gives the possibility for this.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

print(df.groupby('Year'))
print(df.groupby('Year')['Metascore'].mean())

<pandas.core.groupby.generic.DataFrameGroupBy object at 0x0000015112A26520>
Year

2007    63.924528

2014    57.614583
2015    57.000000

Name: Metascore, dtype: float64

The example shows that as a result of the grouping we do not get a table as a result, but a new special object from which we can call aggregating functions along the individual columns. The result of the aggregations, however, is already a list.

Let us take a more complex example:

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('imdb.csv', index_col='Title')

df = df.sort_values(['Revenue (Millions)'])
df = df.reset_index() # Puts the index back as a column; without this we could not query the Title value later
df_by_year_dir = df.groupby(['Year', 'Director'])

result = pd.DataFrame()
result['Year'] = df_by_year_dir['Year'].first()
result['Director'] = df_by_year_dir['Director'].first()
result['Best movie'] = df_by_year_dir['Title'].last()
result['Best revenue'] = df_by_year_dir['Revenue (Millions)'].max()
result['Total revenue'] = df_by_year_dir['Revenue (Millions)'].sum()
result['Number of films'] = df_by_year_dir['Director'].count()

result = result[result['Number of films'] > 1]

print(result)

In the example we formed groups along the year and director columns, then looked at which was the director's best film in the given year, how much revenue it brought in, how much the total revenue of the director's films was in that year, and how many films the director had in the given year. After this we filtered the list so that only the data of directors with more than one film in a given year would appear.

Into the first two columns we took the year and the director of the given category. The first function is needed, since these are lists in which the value belonging to the group is repeated as many times as the number of elements of the group, but we only want to display one. These two columns are in fact unnecessary, because these values appear in the indices.

Earlier we put the list in increasing order by revenue, so of the titles we queried the last value in order to get the film with the highest revenue. We put the title of the film back into the table with the reset_index function, because after the grouping the original index would be lost.

After this we calculated the maximum and the sum of the revenue in the given group, then counted the elements. The latter can be counted on any column, but care has to be taken, because it does not count the NaN values. So if one of our columns is not completely filled in, the count may return false information.

Data-type-specific functions

The dtypes property shows which data type is found in which column. An important additional point is that when we read in the data, Pandas decides on the basis of the first few rows what data type is in the column (one column, one type). This can often lead to errors when reading in, or, for example, it happens that numbers are stored as text.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

display(df.head())
display(df.dtypes)

The general function for changing the data type is the astype() function.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

df['Year'].astype('int')

0         1992
1         2012
2         1920
3         1900
4         1988
          ... 
271111    1976
271112    2014
271113    2014
271114    1998
271115    2002
Name: Year, Length: 271116, dtype: int32

Date type

The date data type requires special handling; the function below would work correctly if the data were given in the format YYYY-MM-DD HH:MM:SS.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

df['Year'].astype('datetime64[s]')

0        1970-01-01 00:33:12
1        1970-01-01 00:33:32
2        1970-01-01 00:32:00
3        1970-01-01 00:31:40
4        1970-01-01 00:33:08
                 ...        
271111   1970-01-01 00:32:56
271112   1970-01-01 00:33:34
271113   1970-01-01 00:33:34
271114   1970-01-01 00:33:18
271115   1970-01-01 00:33:22
Name: Year, Length: 271116, dtype: datetime64[ns]

The result is indeed of date type, but without the appropriate conversion the function did not recognise that the given number denoted the year, so it calculated with the given unit, the second. Pandas' own conversion function is to_datetime(), in which we can also give the format as a parameter. And from data given in date format the date and the time parts can be extracted separately with the dt suffix, as well as such data as the number of the week (dt.isocalendar().week) or whether the given year is a leap year (dt.is_leap_year).

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

df['Year'] = pd.to_datetime(df['Year'], format='%Y')

display(df['Year'])
display(df['Year'].dt.date)
display(df['Year'].dt.time)
display(df['Year'].dt.isocalendar().week)
display(df['Year'].dt.is_leap_year)

Text type

The suffix of the text type is str, on which we can call a great many further functions. A few examples, without any claim to completeness:

  • lower() / upper() - the lower- and upper-case versions of the text
  • zfill() - pads the text with 0s. This can come in handy if, for example, we want to create a unique identifier
  • startswith() - with its help we can search for texts having a certain beginning (the result is the set of the corresponding indices)
  • contains() - with its help we can search for texts containing a piece of text (the result is the set of the corresponding indices)
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

print('LOWER')
display(df['Event'].str.lower())
print('ZFILL')
display(df['Event'].str.zfill(width=30))
print('STARTSWITH')
display(df.loc[df['Event'].str.startswith('Basket')])
print('CONTAINS')
print(len(df.loc[df['Event'].str.contains('Men')])) # We only print the count

The contains function is able to handle so-called regular expressions. A regular expression (abbreviated: regexp or regex) is a string written according to certain syntactic rules with which a set of strings can be determined.

Such an expression can be used for searching for or replacing text according to some pattern, or for validating text data.

For example, a valid transaction reference certainly consists of the following elements:

  1. a digit between 1 and 8 (the code of the trading desk);
  2. a space;
  3. 19 or 20 or 21 and two more digits (year);
  4. after that
  5. a 0 and a digit between 1 and 9, or
  6. a 1 and a digit between 0 and 2 (month);
  7. a digit between 0 and 2 and a digit between 0 and 9, or
  8. a 3 followed by 0 or 1 (day)
  9. a space
  10. and four more digits.

On the pythex site we can test our regex expressions interactively. Below are a few more examples of special regex expressions.

In the following query, which also contains a regex, we searched on the basis of a regex (regex=True), disregarded upper and lower case (case=False), and selected only those rows in which the expression “women” appears, followed by “ball”, in such a way that any number of other characters may occur between the two.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

df.loc[df['Event'].str.contains('women.*ball', regex=True, case=False)]

The split() function, similarly to Python's built-in version, splits the text on the basis of the given character. With the expand parameter it puts the result straight into separate columns containing the elements.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

df['Games'].str.split(' ', expand=True)

Numeric type

In Pandas the two basic numeric types (int, float) are present, but beyond these it can also handle more sophisticated numpy number formats. The problem with the basic astype() function is that in the case of int conversion it cannot handle the missing elements. Such values are by default replaced by Pandas with a nan value, which is in fact a numpy-based np.nan value. When we print it to the screen, it appears uniformly as NaN.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

df['Age'].astype('int')

---------------------------------------------------------------------------
...

IntCastingNaNError: Cannot convert non-finite values (NA or inf) to integer

With the isnull() or isna() functions already known from earlier we can search for the missing values. It is important that nan values will not match in the case of a comparison.

import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

print(np.nan == np.nan)
df.loc[df['Age'].isna()]

The correct way of converting is the to_numeric() function, with which the incorrect values can also be handled, alongside other features.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

pd.to_numeric(df['Age'])

0         24.0
1         23.0
2         24.0
3         34.0
4         21.0
          ... 
271111    29.0
271112    27.0
271113    27.0
271114    30.0
271115    34.0
Name: Age, Length: 271116, dtype: float64

Categorical type

The categorical type comes in handy in statistical analyses, and memory can also be saved with it. For example, it is worth storing sex in this format.

import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv('olimpia.csv')

df['Medal'] = df['Medal'].fillna('Participation').astype('category')
display(df['Medal'])

0         Participation
1         Participation
2         Participation
3                  Gold
4         Participation
              ...      
271111    Participation
271112    Participation
271113    Participation
271114    Participation
271115    Participation
Name: Medal, Length: 271116, dtype: category
Categories (4, object): ['Bronze', 'Gold', 'Participation', 'Silver']

With the cat suffix the special categorical functions can be reached. The categories property, for example, shows the existing categories. A categorical type can be ordered. This is suitable, for example, for storing the answers no, slightly no, slightly yes, yes.

Exercises

szeged.csv

  1. Read in the szeged.csv file. Look at its first few rows and the size of the whole database, and print the descriptive statistics and the correlation between the columns.
  2. Delete the “Loud Cover” and “Daily Summary” columns. Rename the remaining columns so that each is lower case and the words are separated by _ !
  3. Look at which day the visibility was greatest! What was the average humidity? On which day was the difference between the temperature and the apparent temperature greatest?
  4. How many rows are there where snow fell, the description indicates foggy weather, and either the visibility was between 0 and 20 metres, or the visibility was above 3.2 km but the humidity was below 0.9?
  5. Display what the average temperature was by weather type (Precip Type)!

olimpia.csv

  1. Let us find out in which event the 3 oldest Olympians competed, and how old they were!
  2. Let us find out in which event the 3 heaviest Olympians competed, and how many kg they were!
  3. Let us find which 10 countries had the most participants in the history of the Olympics (someone who attended the Olympics three times is counted three times)!
  4. *Hard: Let us find which 10 countries have the most Olympians (one person is counted once)!
  5. Let us find which 10 countries have the most medals, regardless of colour!
  6. *Hard: Let us find, among the competitors of the 10 countries with the most medals, those who were older than 60 at one of their Olympics!
  7. Which country had the youngest Olympians on average? And the heaviest?
  8. How do the average age and body weight of Olympians who won no medal and of gold, silver and bronze medallists compare with one another?
  9. Let us collect the list of discontinued Olympic sports and the last year in which they appeared!
  10. How many Hungarian gold medals were won?
  11. Print the data of the oldest participant!
  12. Collect which sport first appeared at which Olympics!
  13. Calculate how many people in total competed at the Olympics from each country!

covid.csv

  1. Print how many days' data appear in the table for each country! (value_counts)
  2. Calculate for every day, and save into a new column, what proportion of the vaccinated people (people_vaccinated) are those with full vaccination (people_fully_vaccinated)!
  3. Filter the data set to the Hungarian data and save this into a new dataframe!
  4. Print, with reference to the Hungarian data, what the observed period was (first and last date)!
  5. How many Hungarian fatalities were there in total in the observed period?
